I am seventy-two years old and have tilled the land in Quzhou County for more than fifty years. Because I finished high school, I can read the county’s agricultural bulletins and understand the extension recommendations better than many of my neighbors. On the North China Plain, the climate and groundwater allow two crops a year, so the only sensible choice for my family’s eight mu is the winter wheat–summer maize rotation. I do not experiment with strange crops at my age; I stick to what the market and the weather guarantee.

My wheat, sown last October, is already in the ground. I use Jimai 22, an improved variety that has proven itself here for over a decade. This spring I will manage it carefully: three irrigations—at green-up, heading and grain-filling—and about thirty-five kilograms of nitrogen per mu, mostly as urea top-dressed at jointing. I also apply compound fertilizer to supply phosphorus and potassium. I plan four pesticide sprays in total (herbicide once, insecticide twice, fungicide once) to keep aphids and powdery mildew under control. I expect roughly 550 kg per mu.

After the wheat harvest in early June, I will immediately plant Denghai 605 hybrid maize using no-tillage directly into the wheat stubble. At my age, speed and labor saving are vital; no-tillage lets me catch the summer heat without exhausting myself. I will apply about fifteen kilograms of nitrogen per mu for the maize—slightly more than the village average because I know the crop needs it after the wheat has depleted the soil—plus four kilograms each of phosphorus and potassium. Two irrigations should suffice if the summer rains are normal, and I will spray pesticides three times to control weeds and corn borers. I target 600 kg per mu.
